items.title: Black Queer and Trans Men in Online Environments: Information Practices, Affordances, and Platform Constraints
items.abstract: This study examines how Black queer and trans men navigate online environments to seek information, manage visibility, and build community amid intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, and power. It asks how platform affordances and constraints shape their information practices and opportunities for participation. The research combines semi-structured interviews with critical technocultural discourse analysis (CTDA). Thirty-four Black queer and trans men participated in interviews, with 12 selected for in-depth analysis. CTDA examined three digital artifacts: Hoodrat to Headwrap, PHAG TAWLK, and TS Madison’s “Protect the Children All the Way Around.” Black ontology, intersectionality, and epistemic resistance inform the analysis of participants’ experiences and the cultural and technological contexts of these artifacts. Three interrelated findings emerge from the interview data: Platform navigation, visibility management, and community connection. Participants made strategic decisions about where and how to engage online. Visibility was negotiated across platforms and audiences. Across both datasets, race, gender, and masculinity were understood through lived experience, relationships, social expectations, and histories of racialized and gendered treatment. Platforms are sites of sociotechnical power, shaping participation, circulation, and whose knowledge becomes legible. The podcasts and their comment spaces also show that meaning is produced not only by creators but negotiated with audiences. This study expands information practices to include knowledge exchange, identity work, care, critique, and visibility management. Platform governance shapes information practice, influencing trust, participation, and what kinds of information circulate. Black transness is an analytic position , revealing how racialized and gendered hierarchies shape legitimacy, participation, and digital futures.

items.title: Black Queer and Trans Men Online Environments: Information Practices, Affordances and Platform Constraints
items.abstract: Digital environments can marginalize Black queer and trans men while also providing vital spaces for information exchange, identity work, and community connection. Although scholarship examines marginalized communities' digital experiences, the information practices of Black queer and trans men remain understudied. This study examines how Black queer and trans men navigate sociotechnical systems that shape visibility, participation, and belonging, with particular attention to how platform conditions shape information practices. This study uses 34 semi-structured interviews with Black queer and trans men, including 12 selected for in-depth analysis, and digital media artifacts examined through Critical Technocultural Discourse Analysis (CTDA). The research examines how participants create, interpret, share, and manage information across digital environments, including decisions about when and how to engage with others. The study uses Black ontology, intersectionality, and epistemic resistance as a conceptual framework to guide the analysis of semi-structured interviews and digital media artifacts through CTDA. The analysis identifies three themes: Platform Navigation, Visibility Management, and Community Connection. Participants negotiate platform affordances and constraints while managing visibility in response to racialized and gendered surveillance. They also cultivate alternative information ecologies through care, knowledge exchange, and collective resistance in online communities. The study expands information practices beyond seeking and retrieval to include identity work, critique, and visibility management. Platform governance shapes trust, participation, and information circulation. Black transness serves as an analytic lens that reveals how racialized and gendered hierarchies shape knowledge, legitimacy, and digital futures, with implications for information science and more equitable platform governance.

items.title: Boundaries for generative AI use and task delegation in nursing education: a scoping review with critical evidence synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education, but studies rarely evaluate task delegation explicitly. This review mapped evidence on educational tasks, contexts of use, and safeguards to inform boundaries for using large language models (LLMs) and delegating educational tasks. Methods This scoping review with critical evidence synthesis used JBI guidance for evidence mapping and PRISMA-ScR for reporting. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 7 August 2026 for studies involving direct interaction between prelicensure nursing students and LLM-based systems. The review team extracted outcomes, risks, safeguards, and human oversight. The team proposed delegation statuses by considering the consequences of error, error detectability under specified safeguards, the need for human judgment, confidence in the evidence, and oversight feasibility. Results Of the 440 records screened, 46 studies comprising 47 educational application profiles were included. Of the 146 outcome records, 115 were favorable, 13 were mixed, 10 showed no difference, 6 were unfavorable, and 2 were unclear. Twelve studies (26.1%) reported at least one objectively verified error or event or an adverse educational outcome. Among the 118 safeguards, 100 (84.7%) were proposed or implemented without evaluation beyond implementation, five (4.2%) were evaluated for feasibility or acceptability, and 13 (11.0%) were evaluated for risk reduction. The proposed matrix comprises 16 task categories: eight conditionally delegable, five restricted to a supportive role, two unsuitable for automated delegation, and one with insufficient evidence. Conclusion The matrix offers a preliminary framework for task-specific decisions. Bounded knowledge support and low-risk formative feedback may be conditionally delegable with appropriate safeguards and oversight. AI should support clinical reasoning and care planning, whereas final grading, competence decisions, and ethical judgment should remain human responsibilities. The matrix requires validation and updating as direct evidence, particularly on safeguard effectiveness, becomes available. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

items.title: Brand Impersonation and Customer Support Hijacking Analysing How Fraudulent Customer Service Accounts on Social Media Scam Corporate Clients
items.abstract: Social media is a public-facing channel for customer-service, and brands are now able to respond to questions and complaints quickly. Consumers' visibility also enables scams to monitor consumers, replicate brand identities and approach consumers via replies or private messages. This article will discuss the methods used by fraudulent customer support accounts to leverage brand recognition and social trust, and will assess controls at the user, company, platform and payment levels. This focused narrative review collated 29 scholarly papers from 2020-2026, comprising of 21 journal papers and eight peer-reviewed conference papers. The evidence shows brand impersonation is not just a fake-profile problem of classification. It's a multi-step fraud route that includes squatting on an account, timely interception of support requests, transferring to private or external channels, requests for credentials, verification codes or payment. Machine-learning studies provide helpful indicators from profile content, profile behavior and network structure, and human-factors studies explain why social familiarity and perceived authenticity can make a difference in reducing scrutiny. Most detection studies rely on labels and data sets, however, that are not inherently linked to customer-support impersonation or financial loss. The article suggests a multi-layered approach to the response, incorporating the official channel clarity of guidance, fast reporting of evidence for preservation, behaviour-awareness in platform detection, safer support channels and metrics for success like time to takedown and repeat-account activity. The review offers a practical approach for minimising the risk of customer harm, as well as opportunities for research in cross-platform measurement and in the field.

items.title: Building AI-Ready Infrastructure for Scientific User Facilities
items.abstract: Autonomous experimentation is emerging across materials synthesis, synchrotron and neutron characterization, real-time data analysis, and scientific decision-making. Yet increasingly capable artificial intelligence does not by itself create autonomous science. Scientific user facilities must also provide machine-operable experiments, machine-readable data and interoperable interfaces, persistent provenance across the experimental lifecycle, scientific capabilities that can be discovered and orchestrated across instruments and facilities, and access models compatible with iterative experimental campaigns. We argue that these infrastructure requirements should be treated as a coupled scientific design problem. Their value is not limited to higher throughput: reducing the latency between observation, interpretation, decision, and the next measurement can enable more effective exploration of metastable states, competing phases and phase coexistence, degradation and failure pathways, phase boundaries, and other difficult-to-access phenomena. Drawing on recent demonstrations in autonomous laboratories and advanced characterization, along with discussions from the 2026 Advanced Light Source Automation and Self-Driving Labs Workshop, we outline a practical progression from automated instruments to distributed autonomous discovery ecosystems that link synthesis, synchrotron and neutron characterization, computing, theory, and human scientific judgment.

items.title: Building Information Modelling (BIM) for Fire Safety: Potentials, Tools and Research Gaps
items.abstract: Fire risk in the built environment has increased with rapid urbanization, population growth and technological developments, requiring an interdisciplinary approach to fire safety throughout the building life cycle. Building Information Modelling (BIM) offers significant potential for fire safety design, performance-based analysis, project management and interdisciplinary collaboration. This paper aims to emphasize the support that BIM can provide to students, researchers, designers and engineers working in the field of building design for fire safety. The potentials of BIM tools are investigated and categorized according to their purpose of use in the collaborative process. A comprehensive literature review is conducted in major indexed academic databases as well as an evaluation of widely used BIM tools and plug-ins that are used to support fire safety measures. The results reveal that BIM has primarily been applied to fire safety simulation, evacuation analysis and information management. 3D modelling, real-time collaboration and scenario-based analysis provided in BIM has high potential in improving fire-safety decision-making. However, research remains limited on design decision-making, intelligent technologies, human behavior, urban-scale design and heritage buildings. Future studies need to integrate BIM with digital twins, artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things to create more resilient, sustainable and fire-safe environments.

items.title: Calibration-Free Eye Tracking through Binocular-Constrained Homography Normalization
items.abstract: Implicit user calibration and calibration-free eye-tracking methods have been explored to improve the usability of gaze-based interactions. However, these methods for regression- and model-based approaches typically require multiple observations or camera-display calibration. Therefore, we propose a binocular-constrained homography normalization method that enables calibration-free gaze estimation from a single observation without camera-display calibration. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first homography-based framework to incorporate calibration-free gaze estimation. For each eye, the corneal center and optical axis are estimated using a 3D eyeball model with a monocular camera, and the point-of-gaze is computed using homography transformations derived from both eyes. The proposed method achieved a mean horizontal angular error of 1.01° under the tested conditions. The experimental evaluations supported the feasibility of the proposed method and identified directions for further improvement.

items.title: Can AI Express Sentiment Like Humans in Research Abstracts? Implications for Academic Publishing
items.abstract: Sentiment is widely examined in academic and non‐academic contexts. However, with the advancement of generative artificial intelligence, no study has compared linguistic positivity in AI‐generated and human‐written academic texts. Adopting sentiment analysis, this study compares the sentiment scores of 420 research abstracts published in top journals across 14 hard and soft disciplines with 420 abstracts generated by DeepSeek. Our findings show that DeepSeek‐generated abstracts and human‐written journal abstracts show no significant difference in terms of their sentiment distribution. This pattern is observed across hard and the majority of the soft disciplines. These results indicate that AI‐generated abstracts closely approximate human‐written abstracts in linguistic positivity, as shown in lexicon‐based sentiment scores. Given the findings, this study envisions human‐AI collaboration in future knowledge production and calls for adjustments to current frameworks of academic evaluation.

items.title: Can AI Make with Us? Exploring Tacit Knowledge and Emotion in AI-Supported Making
items.abstract: As AI reshapes how people learn and create, questions arise about forms of knowledge that are embodied, practice-based, and difficult to articulate. This study examines how learners physically co-create with AI and what forms of tacit knowledge emerge through that process. It further investigates how emotions surface and are managed throughout AI-supported making. Through this examination, this study aims to holistically capture the cognitive, emotional, and behavioral dimensions of tacit knowledge acquisition in an AI-supported making environment. We designed and facilitated a pilot workshop centered on e-textile making with community members in Champaign-Urbana, Illinois in April 2026. E-textile was selected for its inherently tactile and embodied nature, offering a deliberate contrast to AI’s text-based, formalized mode of knowledge. Nine participants engaged freely with AI tools of their choice alongside human facilitators, creating a naturalistic environment where both forms of support coexisted. To capture the holistic process of cognition, behavioral patterns, and emotional responses, think-aloud protocols, observation, pre-post surveys, and interviews were used as data collection methods. Preliminary findings reveal no consensus on how AI supported ideation, process, or outcomes, suggesting that its role in tacit-knowledge-rich making is highly individual. Emotionally, participants expressed confidence, curiosity, and surprise throughout the workshops, while also navigating moments of stress and frustration. This study contributes to Library and Information Science understanding of how human-AI collaboration unfolds in spaces where knowledge is socially constructed and physically embodied. It further offers insight into the emotional experiences that emerge and are managed throughout AI-supported learning.

items.title: Can AI Personalise Meaningfulness? Bodies, Prediction, and Postdigital Health and Physical Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly woven into Health and Physical Education (HPE) through motion analysis, wearable data, adaptive task design, automated feedback, and generative support for teachers. These developments are often associated with personalisation and, by extension, with the possibility of making learning more meaningful for individual students. This conceptual article questions that connection. Drawing on Kretchmar’s philosophy of meaning in movement, Meaningful Physical Education (MPE), and postdigital accounts of entangled pedagogy and technological mediation, it argues that meaningfulness is not a personalised output but a postdigital accomplishment. It emerges through embodied activity, relationships, material settings, cultural practices, interpretation, and time. Particular AI-supported arrangements may expand or constrain these conditions, but no technical adjustment can guarantee what an experience will come to mean. The analysis develops four tensions: personal relevance between dialogue and prediction; challenge between embodied negotiation and adaptive optimisation; fun, sociality, and delight beyond engagement analytics; and biographical meaning in relation to computational memory. It shows how personalised systems can also influence whose movements, preferences, and histories become visible and valued. The article concludes with five commitments for keeping meaningfulness open in postdigital HPE: interpretive openness, negotiated personalisation, embodied and relational attentiveness, collective possibility, and temporal and infrastructural humility.

items.title: Cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline: a reciprocal multisystem connection defined by apolipoproteins, sirtuins, and non-coding RNAs
items.abstract: The age of the global population continues to increase with expectations that over the next several decades more than 2 billion individuals will reach the age of 60 or greater. With this increase in lifespan, the prevalence of non-communicable diseases has markedly risen with the disorders of cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline, including Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis, existing at the forefront to impact the world’s population with significant morbidity and mortality. Cardiovascular and cognitive decline disorders are intimately linked through mechanisms of vascular disease, inflammation, metabolic dysfunction, loss of cellular energy stores, and oxidative stress, but despite multi-modality treatments disease progression can continue with the disorders and may involve clinical complications. Given these challenges, innovative treatment strategies are warranted that can address the onset and progression of cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline that involve apolipoproteins, such as apolipoprotein E, sirtuins, such as silent mating type information regulation 2 homolog 1 ( S. cerevisiae ) (SIRT1), SIRT2, SIRT3, and SIRT6, non-coding RNAs, such as microRNAs and circular RNAs, and multisystem networks that entail the gut microbiome and metabolic pathways with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonism. These underlying pathways not only serve to offer new avenues of care, but also offer exciting prospects as diagnostic tools for early disease detection and progression with the use of platforms that employ artificial intelligence and machine learning. Yet, it is critical to recognize that these pathways are complex, tightly dependent upon one another, and are impacted by diverse cellular networks that can ultimately influence biological and clinical outcomes.

items.title: Çeviri Kararını Kim Veriyor? Üretken Yapay Zekâ Destekli Çeviride Eyleyicilik ve Sorumluluk
items.abstract: Üretken yapay zekânın çeviri süreçlerine katılması, geleneksel doğrusal üretim modelini yetersiz bırakmaktadır. Bu modelde çeviriyi yalnızca insan çevirmen gerçekleştirir. Teknoloji ise edilgin bir araç olarak kullanılır. Oysa günümüzde büyük dil modelleri farklı çeviri seçenekleri üretmektedir. Komutlar çıktının biçimini yönlendirmektedir. Platformlar erişim ve kullanım koşullarını belirlerken işverenler hız, maliyet ve kalite beklentilerini tanımlamaktadır. İnsan çevirmen ise üretilen metni seçmekte, düzeltmekte veya onaylamaktadır. Buna rağmen mevcut mesleki ve etik söylem, çevirinin sonucundan doğan sorumluluğu çoğunlukla son metni onaylayan çevirmene yüklemektedir. Bu çalışma, yapay zekâ destekli çeviride eyleyiciliğin farklı aktörler arasında dağılması ile sorumluluğun tek bir insan özne üzerinde yoğunlaşması arasındaki kuramsal çelişkiyi incelemektedir. Çalışmanın amacı, çevirmen eyleyiciliğini insan–makine karşıtlığının ötesinde yeniden tanımlamaktır. Ayrıca çeviri sürecindeki denetim ve sorumluluk ilişkisini açıklayabilecek kavramsal bir model geliştirmek amaçlanmaktadır. Çalışmada eleştirel kavramsal çözümleme ve bütünleştirici alanyazın değerlendirmesi kullanılmaktadır. Çevirmen eyleyiciliğine ilişkin tartışmalar; eleştirel insan-sonrası yaklaşım, çeviri etiği, insan merkezli yapay zekâ ve dağıtılmış eyleyicilik çerçevesinde ele alınmaktadır. Bu doğrultuda insan çevirmenin, büyük dil modelinin, komutun, eğitim verisinin, dijital platformun, işverenin ve editörün çeviri kararındaki konumları karşılaştırılmaktadır. Kuramsal çözümleme sonucunda “Dağıtılmış Eyleyicilik ve Orantılı Sorumluluk Modeli” önerilmektedir. Model, çeviri sürecini dört düzeyde ele almaktadır. İlk düzey, çeviri seçeneklerinin üretilmesidir. İkinci düzey, bu seçeneklerin dayandığı bilginin denetlenebilmesidir. Üçüncü düzey, nihai kararın verilmesidir. Son düzey ise kararın sonuçlarının gerekçelendirilebilmesidir. Yapay zekâ sisteminin çeviri üretimine nedensel ve işlemsel olarak katılması, ona kendiliğinden etik sorumluluk kazandırmamaktadır. Ancak insan çevirmen de modelin eğitim verilerine, çalışma mantığına ve kurumsal kullanım koşullarına çoğunlukla erişememektedir. Bu nedenle bütün sorumluluğun çevirmene yüklenmesi kuramsal olarak savunulabilir değildir. Çalışma, sorumluluğun yalnızca son metni onaylayan kişiye yüklenemeyeceğini ileri sürmektedir. Sorumluluk; karar yetkisi, denetim kapasitesi ve kurumsal güç dikkate alınarak katmanlı biçimde değerlendirilmelidir. Bu değerlendirme çevirmeni, işvereni, platform sağlayıcısını ve sistem geliştiricisini kapsamalıdır. Bu çerçevede çevirmenin yeni statüsü, yapay zekâ çıktısını düzelten bir son okuyucuyla sınırlandırılamaz. Çevirmen; süreci tasarlayan, riskleri belirleyen, tercihlerini gerekçelendiren ve gerektiğinde makine çıktısını reddedebilen eleştirel bir karar öznesi olarak yeniden tanımlanmalıdır.

items.title: Challenges in Clean-Label Reformulation of Ultra-Processed Foods: Balancing Consumer Expectations, Functionality, and Safety
items.abstract: Demand for foods perceived as natural, lightly processed and clearly labelled has brought clean-label formulation to the forefront of food product development. Concern about preservatives, synthetic additives and possible health implications of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) has encouraged manufacturers to investigate ingredients of natural origin. Reformulation is nevertheless difficult: conventional additives fulfil several interdependent roles in microbial protection, product structure, flavour, stability and shelf life, whereas their proposed replacements may be less consistent, more expensive or less acceptable to consumers. Drawing on literature identified in Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar, this narrative, domain-focused review provides a conceptual discussion rather than a systematic review or quantitative analysis. It examines interpretations of clean label, consumer attitudes, additive functions in UPFs and the barriers encountered when reformulating them. Options considered include botanical preservatives, plant-derived ingredients, fermentation, biotechnological processes, encapsulation and newer food-processing methods. Of these, combinations of natural antimicrobials and preservation hurdles, fermentation-derived ingredients and non-thermal treatments currently have the most established applications. Precision fermentation, nano-encapsulation and artificial intelligence-guided formulation require further validation. Importantly, changing the ingredient list does not automatically change a food's NOVA group 4 classification or improve its nutritional composition. Successful reformulation must therefore reconcile transparent labelling and consumer preferences with demonstrable safety, technological performance, sustainability and economic practicality.

items.title: Chinese Pathologists’ Adoption of Large Language Models: Cross-Sectional Survey on Influencing Factors
items.abstract: Background The growing demand for pathology services and the shortage of pathologists in China have created an urgent need for innovative tools to improve diagnostic efficiency and support professional practice. Large language models (LLMs) may assist pathologists in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education, but their implementation depends on many factors, such as pathologists’ awareness and willingness to adopt these technologies. Objective This study aimed to assess Chinese pathologists’ awareness, practical experience, perceptions, ethical concerns regarding LLMs; their willingness to adopt LLMs; and factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology. Methods A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among certified pathologists practicing in mainland China. The survey assessed participants’ demographic and professional characteristics; LLM awareness, use, and perceived performance in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education; ethical concerns; and suggestions for future improvement. Questionnaire reliability and validity were assessed using Cronbach α, Guttman Lambda 6, and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure. Group differences in perceived performance were examined using Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. Factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology were measured as the summed score of three 5-point Likert items and analyzed using ordinal logistic regression. Results Of 339 eligible pathologists, 248 (73.2%) had heard of LLMs, and 64 of these (25.8%) had used them. ChatGPT was the most recognized and most commonly used model. Compared with nonusers, LLM users rated clinical applications more cautiously, particularly for analyzing patient data, organizing medical history, and supporting the understanding of disease mechanisms and treatments; these differences were significant after domain-specific FDR adjustment (adjusted P=.02) but borderline after overall correction across all performance items (adjusted P=.05). Perceptions of research and educational applications did not differ significantly between users and nonusers. A higher education level, attending physicians (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.39, 95% CI 1.09-5.22; P=.029), chief physicians (aOR 4.64, 95% CI 1.57-13.69; P=.005), and more than 43 weekly working hours (aOR 2.33, 95% CI 1.40-3.89; P=.001) were associated with greater willingness to use LLMs, whereas working in fourth- or lower-tier cities (aOR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.79; P=.007) and reading 1001-3000 slides annually (aOR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20-0.94; P=.034) were associated with less willingness. Major ethical concerns included model transparency, sensitive data security, and academic misuse. Conclusions Chinese pathologists show high awareness of LLMs and generally favorable attitudes toward their potential application in pathology, but actual use is limited. The gap between awareness and use highlights the need for improved accessibility, targeted training, pathology-specific validation, workflow integration, and ethical governance. Future implementation should emphasize locally adapted models, data security, and equitable access, particularly for pathologists in lower-tier cities and resource-limited settings.

items.title: Claim Enlargement Through Familiar Rewording: Why a Rounder Sentence Can Claim More Than the Study Did
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Claim Enlargement Through Familiar Rewording, a mechanism by which a bounded finding is restated in familiar language that appears equivalent but asserts more than the original procedure established. A description tied to particular participants, measures, and conditions can become a general claim when those qualifications disappear. The resulting statement may be easier to understand while supporting conclusions or decisions that the original evidence did not warrant. The paper assesses rewording by reconstructing the procedure that produced the finding, comparing its original description with subsequent formulations, and identifying what each revision adds or omits. Plain language is not itself a defect, and a broader claim may be true on independent evidence. The mechanism concerns the transfer of evidential standing from a narrower statement to a wider one through an apparently ordinary restatement. Its practical significance becomes visible when the revised wording supports action beyond the scope of the original result. The discussion examines two documented cases. In a 1993 study, K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues reported that the strongest group of violin students had accumulated approximately 10,000 hours of solitary practice on average by age twenty. Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers subsequently described the figure as something each elite player had reached and extended its significance across fields. In 2010, photographer Dan McLaughlin left his job to test whether 10,000 hours of deliberate practice could make him a professional golfer. The second case concerns a 1993 experiment involving 36 college students. Researchers reported higher spatial-reasoning scores immediately after participants listened to a Mozart sonata than after comparison conditions. In 1998, Georgia governor Zell Miller described the finding as a nine-point increase in IQ scores while requesting funding to provide classical recordings to families with newborns. The original study had not established a general increase in intelligence or an effect in infants. Part of the Representation and Measurement series within On Human Modeling, the paper places the mechanism alongside published research on exaggeration in university press releases. It examines how evidential limits can disappear as findings move among researchers, intermediaries, and decision-makers. Potential applications in human–AI interaction include automated summarization, research synthesis, generated explanations, and evaluations that test whether paraphrasing preserves the scope of the evidence it reports.

items.title: Clinical AI agents: a short narrative review
items.abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents represent an emerging generation of AI systems. They extend conventional clinical decision support through goal-directed planning, tool interaction and adaptation of actions to intermediate results. Memory may support these functions but is not essential in every implementation. Human oversight is a safeguard for clinical deployment rather than an intrinsic capability. This short narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the core architectural features, representative clinical applications, and primary implementation challenges of clinical AI agents. Recent studies indicate promising applications in diagnostic decision support, workflow automation, patient communication, and evidence synthesis. However, existing evidence remains largely based on technical validation studies, proof-of-concept systems, and conceptual frameworks, with relatively limited prospective evaluation in routine clinical practice. Key challenges include establishing reliable evaluation frameworks, ensuring process-level safety, developing effective governance structures, and generating robust clinical evidence to support implementation. Although technological progress is rapid, widespread adoption will require not only further technical advances but also rigorous clinical validation, transparent governance, and successful integration into healthcare workflows. Clinical AI agents may become useful components of multidisciplinary healthcare workflows, provided that future research addresses the remaining methodological and implementation challenges.

items.title: Cluster-Based Learner Profiling in AI-Supported Educational Contexts: Evidence from Junior High School Students
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational settings, learner heterogeneity can no longer be adequately described through single-variable comparisons. This study identifies learner profiles in AI-supported educational contexts using three theoretically grounded feature dimensions: AI self-efficacy, digital literacy, and cross-disciplinary integration self-efficacy. These dimensions were operationalized using eight indicators reflecting students’ AI-related confidence, digital information-processing competence, and integrative learning readiness. Based on 8,022 valid responses from eighth-grade students in the collaborative database of the Taiwan Assessment of Student Achievement: Longitudinal Study and the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study, available from the Survey Research Data Archive, Academia Sinica, all input indicators were normalized using Z -score scaling to construct a standardized feature space for distance estimation. A two-stage clustering procedure was adopted. First, two-step cluster analysis was performed to compare candidate solutions based on Akaike Information Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion values; subsequently, K -means clustering was conducted with the number of clusters fixed at six to estimate the final learner profiles. The results supported six profiles: high-scoring integrated; very low-scoring; AI-moderate, digitally weak; broadly below-average; digitally adequate, AI-integration weak; and near-average balanced. The profiles showed that learner heterogeneity was not organized along a simple high–low continuum but appeared as asymmetric configurations within the multidimensional feature space. Post-clustering analyses further showed that digital-literacy indicators and AI evaluation had the largest descriptive between-profile separations, and that cluster membership differed significantly by gender. The findings extend AI literacy research from average-based comparisons to cluster-based learner profiling and provide a basis for differentiated educational support and data-driven decision-making in AI-related educational settings.

items.title: Collaboration to Constraint: Rethinking Generative Artificial Intelligence in User Experience & Interface Design
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have become a standard in the User Experience (UX) & User Interface (UI) design workflows. There has been a shift in Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems reshaping how designers ideate, research, generate layouts, and refine interfaces. These AI systems promise speed and creativity within the UX workflows, but the increase in AI integration has raised questions around control and autonomy shift when they are used for design generation. In this thesis I have investigated the design outcomes when AI is positioned as a creative collaborator, influencing the decision authority and cognitive ownership. In this study, I have used research-through-design combining with auto-ethnography reflections, comparative user interface generation experiments (including Lovable AI-based website creations), and participatory engagements like Open Studio activity and a co-design workshop. The findings suggested that introducing AI early in the design process can lead the design to a specific framework, hierarchy and interaction pattern that narrow divergence. Designers can experience a drift in cognitive ownership while retaining their decision authority when authorship is distributed across prompts, iterations, and AI-generated drafts. In my experiments, AI outputs were polished and plausible but converged towards a similar structural layout. It reflected the influence of dominant pattern in their training data. This thesis argues for responsible integration of AI through careful timing, clear override options, and tools that make AI-driven influence visible, instead of rejecting it completely.

items.title: CoMotion: A Real-Time System for User-Driven Semantic Steering in Text-to-Motion Generation
items.abstract: Current text-to-motion frameworks typically operate as a rigid, one-shot workflow where users are unable to intervene during the generation process, effectively limiting all refinement efforts to the iterative modification of the text prompt. This black-box process hinders iterative design, leading to inefficiency. Furthermore, natural language inherently suffers from ambiguity when describing fine-grained 3D motions, making it difficult for users to articulate their intent solely through text precisely. In this paper, we propose CoMotion , a real-time system that shifts the interaction paradigm from static text prompting to user-driven semantic steering. Instead of requiring users to restart the entire generation process for every modification, CoMotion operates directly within a discrete latent space by retrieving prompt-relevant atomic actions and presenting them as user-visible, adjustable controls. Through CoMotion , users can adjust semantic steering levels for these atomic actions to guide the generation toward their intent without the computational overhead of full text-to-motion model re-inference. Our approach provides a more diverse design pathway for the traditional one-shot text-to-motion generation process, enabling fine-grained, personalized motion control during generation. We validate our system using a standardized benchmark based on Large Language Models. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that CoMotion enables robust semantic correction and geometric diversity while maintaining the kinematic quality of the generated motions. Crucially, by transforming complex generative tasks into low-latency, interactive operations, CoMotion supports an interactive refinement workflow for the evaluated motion generation tasks.

items.title: COMPARATIVE ASSESSMENT OF OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH HAZARDS AMONG WOMEN CASHEW WORKERS IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS OF KERALA
items.abstract: Cashew processing is one of Kerala’s oldest agro-based industries, and its workforce is overwhelmingly female. The work involves handling caustic shell oil, squatting for long hours and repeating the same hand movements thousands of times a day, yet little comparative evidence exists on how these hazards differ between public and private sector units. This paper compares the occupational health of women cashew workers in the two sectors using primary data collected in 2024 from 401 workers (116 in public and 285 in private units) in 50 factories in Kollam district. Chi-square tests, independent-sample t-tests and binary logistic regression were used. About 94 per cent of the women reported at least one health problem (95.1 per cent in private and 90.5 per cent in public units); the difference between sectors was not statistically significant, but the difference across categories of work was (peeling 96.2 per cent, shelling 93.1 per cent, grading 86.2 per cent). Musculoskeletal pain was the most common complaint in both sectors, while respiratory, skin and urinary complaints were concentrated among shelling workers, and public sector workers reported every listed problem more often than their private sector counterparts. Workers who reported health problems rated workplace safety, work-life balance and work conditions lower, had a lower socio-economic index and were older. In the logistic model the work condition index, socio-economic index and category of work were not individually significant, although the model as a whole was (χ² = 13.94, p = 0.008). The results point to the need for ergonomic seating, ventilation, protective equipment and regular health surveillance in cashew factories of both sectors.

items.title: Comparison of AI-Assisted and Conventional Learning in Sustainable Geotechnical Engineering Education-case study on earthen heritage conservation
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) support for sustainable geotechnical engineering education was investigated through a single earthen heritage conservation case study. Data from the eight classes were analyzed, and both the AI-assisted and the traditional groups had 96 student records. The six 90-minute teaching sessions were organized in three weeks. The AI-assisted group and the traditional group were given the same case and teaching time and assessment. The total points available for the 100-point general test and the 80-point sustainability assessment were 180. In addition, the learning outcomes of sustainable geotechnical engineering were also evaluated in four separate learning areas: conceptual understanding, routine calculation, engineering analysis and transfer, each with a maximum score of 100 points. Composite scores showed that the AI-assisted advantage was 17.14 points immediately after the intervention and dropped to 15.29 points four weeks later. The largest between-group differences in all learning areas were found in engineering analysis and transfer. The difference was 9.43 and 9.83 points immediately after the lesson and 7.35 and 9.31 points four weeks later. On the other hand, the participation rate of the AI-assisted group was 82.2%, and that of the traditional group was 63.2%. However, classroom feedback indicated lower independent correction retention in the AI-assisted group, at 71.0% compared with 83.8% in the conventional group. Based on the above results, organised AI support was associated with higher overall achievement and more extensive classroom participation; however, the independent effect of corrected reasoning has not been determined.

items.title: Conditioned connectomes outperform the standard correlation kernel for predicting cognition in an independent cohort
items.abstract: Connectome-based cognition predictions are scored differently across papers. We re-scored a public Human Connectome Project benchmark (753 subjects, six fMRI modalities, 60 family-aware splits) as its authors do, with a public age band in place of exact age, and evaluated a kernel ridge pipeline that conditions each subject's connectome and filters the between-subject kernel's spectrum. With fixed settings it reached r = 0.7215, against 0.6779 for the benchmark paper's best model and 0.6798 for our re-run of its kernel (corrected t = 3.23). This margin is transductive: the filter uses all subjects' unlabelled features, helps only after conditioning, and gives no significant gain fitted on training subjects alone; without it, the difference was not significant. On 263 HCP subjects outside the benchmark, most used in development, a pre-registered comparison favoured the filtered pipeline, computed with them present, over the benchmark's kernel by 0.064 (95% interval 0.030 to 0.099). In an independent cohort never used in development (1,290 adults aged 36 to 89, resting state), the conditioned connectome, fitted on training subjects only, beat the benchmark's kernel as pre-registered (r = 0.5861 against 0.5257; corrected t = 5.47); the filter added nothing there. Against a frozen fMRI foundation model on identical splits, the unfiltered pipeline was ahead in 7 of 8 settings, significantly on resting state (corrected t = 3.88), held-out subjects and ABIDE autism diagnosis, and nominally in AOMIC. Of 18 pre-registered single-decision contrasts, 9 were met, 5 by counting repeats. Two scoring choices each reversed a method ordering.

items.title: Connecting AI Literacy and Copyright Awareness in Undergraduate Education: A Curriculum and Syllabus Review
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised new copyright questions, particularly regarding AI-generated content (Samuelson, 2023). For undergraduate students in Information Sciences (IS) and related fields, understanding these issues is becoming increasingly important. These students may engage in library or other information service-related work in the future and need to deal with the use of AI-generated content and the copyright issues involved. However, how AI and copyright are addressed in undergraduate education remains unclear. Drawing on publicly available course syllabi and descriptions from large U.S. higher education institutions offering IS programs, the study considers how these topics are addressed individually and whether courses discuss copyright issues related to AI-generated content. The findings show that some courses cover AI or copyright topics, but fewer courses discuss how AI-generated content relates to copyright. These findings suggest that undergraduate IS programs could give more attention to copyright issues associated with AI, particularly in courses that already introduce AI technologies. As AI tools become increasingly common in students' academic work, students need to understand not only how to use these tools but also the copyright implications of their use. Therefore, this study highlights the importance of integrating AI literacy, copyright awareness, and ethical reasoning into undergraduate IS education.

items.title: Consequential Human Agency in AI-Enabled Higher Education: Capability, Institutional Authority, and the Right to Contest
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying longstanding questions about the purposes of higher education, the authority of human judgment, and the university's obligations to society. This conceptual, theory-building article argues that AI competence is educationally insufficient when learners lack institutional conditions that make judgment consequential. Drawing on AI-literacy scholarship, ecological theories of agency, democratic education, the capabilities approach, and critical educational technology, it develops an ecological framework of Consequential Human Agency. The framework distinguishes individual capability from agency achieved in interaction with institutional authority, rights to contest and appeal, accountability, and material conditions of participation. Ethical, civic, professional, and leadership agency are treated as contexts of enactment rather than stages or measurable competencies. The article argues that universities are not benign guarantors of agency: as purchasers of platforms, assessment authorities, and users of surveillance and analytics, they can enable or constrain it. Higher education should therefore cultivate judgment while establishing institutional rights and procedures through which students and faculty can question, override, appeal, and help govern consequential AI-mediated decisions.

items.title: Constrained Choice Developing Into Preference Under an Identical Record: Why a Habit Begun Without Options Can Become a Real Preference
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Constrained Choice Developing Into Preference Under an Identical Record, a distinction between repeated behavior that registers a continuing constraint and the same behavior that reflects a preference formed through experience. A record of choices can remain identical while the reasons for those choices change. What began as an obligation may become something a person genuinely wants, just as an activity repeated for years may cease when alternatives become available. The paper assesses this distinction through the alternatives available at different times, the person's choices when those alternatives change, and their own account of what the activity has come to mean. Repetition alone cannot establish preference, and a constrained origin does not invalidate a later liking. Continued or renewed participation under feasible alternatives can support a formed-preference interpretation, particularly when accompanied by evidence of self-directed pursuit. The discussion sets this distinction beside Jon Elster's account of adaptive preferences, separating adjustment to constraint from learning and preference formation through experience. Two documented biographical cases illustrate the distinction. Czech pianist Tomáš Kačo recalls practicing piano throughout childhood because his father required it, describing the experience as an obligation until approximately age fifteen. After developing his own interest, he applied to a conservatory despite his parents' opposition. When rejected, he attended an agricultural school while traveling weekly for lessons in preparation for another audition. Chinese tennis player Li Na entered a state sports program as a child without choosing tennis herself. In 2002 she left the sport to study journalism, returning to competition in 2004. She later described tennis as something she had come to enjoy and pursue for herself. The accounts distinguish externally sustained activity from later choices made under changed conditions. Part of the Formation and Enactment series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who interprets repeated choices, who controls the available alternatives, and who may revise a stored account of another person's preferences. Potential applications in human–AI research include preference learning, personalization, recommendation systems, and evaluations that distinguish behavior produced by restricted options from preferences users have subsequently formed or rejected.

items.title: Continuing Education as Ethical Infrastructure: Informal AI Learning in Academic Librarianship
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic librarianship, requiring sustained ethical, evaluative, and instructional learning. Drawing on interviews with fourteen U.S. STEM academic librarians and scholarship on AI literacy and professional development, this paper examines how librarians develop AI competence through experimentation, peer networks, and personal knowledge management amid uneven institutional support. These conditions shift the costs of adaptation onto individual practitioners and raise concerns about equity, labor, and sustainability. The paper reframes continuing education as sociotechnical infrastructure for AI learning, identifies informal learning as structurally compelled labor, and proposes a role for library and information science (LIS) educators in designing ethical, collaborative, and sustained professional learning. Practice-based pathways, communities of practice, protected learning time, and institutional governance can support critical judgment as AI systems change.
